analysis.title: US Daily: October FOMC Recap: Sticking to an Every-Other-Meeting Pace
key_insights: The FOMC left the funds rate unchanged at its October meeting, a widely expected decision. Fed officials' recent comments had pointed to a compromise of hiking every other meeting, and the meeting gave little reason to expect a deviation from that plan.
GS continues to expect a second and final hike in December, which would leave the funds rate at 4-4.25%. A third hike in March is also possible if inflation comes in higher than GS expects.

The main change to the post-meeting statement is the addition of 'the accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine' the appropriate policy stance. GS reads it as a soft nod toward a slower pace of tightening, because it could imply that decisions need more information than is available between consecutive meetings.

Chairman Warsh's comments were balanced and consistent with both a every-other-meeting pace and a limited total number of hikes. He said neither he nor most other FOMC participants thought the economy was running too hot or that 'economic growth is causing inflation or making our job harder'.
Warsh cited strong business investment growth, a pickup in job growth relative to last year, and jobless claims at 'the lowest level in generations'.

Asked why the Fed did not hike today, Warsh said inflation compensation and inflation expectations had moved in the right direction and that the FOMC had already 'removed a dose of accommodation' at the last meeting.

Warsh said rate hikes are already having an effect and that financial conditions have tightened but are not tight, broadly as expected from the hikes so far. GS's own financial conditions index has evolved the same way over the last two months. His conclusion that 'policy is working' suggests to GS that he is likely to see a limited number of hikes as sufficient.
Warsh gave the Fed task forces a deadline of the end of this year and expects most to report by then. The FOMC would then consider their conclusions and possible changes to Fed policy in 2027Q1.

The FOMC will keep eight meetings per year. Starting next fall, one meeting in 2027 and two in 2028 will be devoted to broad monetary policy strategy, with no policy statement and no vote on the federal funds rate.

vol_and_positioning: GS sees no new information in the October meeting that would change the expected path, so the December hike is the next decision point for rates.
